transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, yeah… I guess I came in because something felt different from normal stress. I’m an artist, and I was working on this memorial piece for my aunt, and I kept getting these awful thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like if I put one photo in the wrong place, or chose the wrong color, it would mean I didn’t love her enough.

And I know that sounds… kind of dramatic when I say it out loud. I’ve had creative doubts before — everyone does, especially with personal work — but this didn’t feel like that. I couldn’t really brush it off. It just kept coming back.

Can you tell me more about those thoughts? Specifically, did they feel like they were coming into your mind against your will, and did you find yourself trying to push them away or do something to neutralize them?

Yeah… they definitely felt unwanted. It wasn’t like I was sitting there thoughtfully deciding, “Oh, maybe this color doesn’t work.” It was more like this sharp thought would just barge in — like, if I put the photo there, it means I’m being careless with her memory, or if I chose the wrong shade, it meant I didn’t love her enough.

And I kept trying to sort of… undo the feeling, I guess. Like reassure myself it was fine, or rethink the piece again. Which is funny because in art school we were always taught to question choices, but this didn’t feel like critique. It felt heavier than that. I couldn’t just brush it off the way I normally would with creative doubts.

Have you found yourself doing any specific actions or going through certain mental steps repeatedly because of these thoughts, like checking, redoing parts of the artwork, or trying to 'reset' your mind in a particular way?

Yeah, I think so. I’ll reread the label text for the piece over and over, even if I literally just read it and know the words are fine. And I’ll nudge the same objects on the table — like a photo or a small frame — just a tiny bit, then move it back, then check it again.

Sometimes I take layout photos on my phone and keep comparing them, which sounds normal for art-making, I guess. I mean, artists document things all the time — I have whole folders of process shots from old projects that I keep meaning to organize, and then I never do. But with this, it’s more like I’m checking until it feels… settled. Like something in me finally lets go for a second.

Part of me knows the layout is already fine. It’s not that I’m making it better each time. I’m just losing studio time doing the same little checks.
Do you feel anxious or upset if you aren't able to do those checks or mental steps, like if something interrupts you or you try to stop yourself?

Yeah… I do get pretty uncomfortable if I try not to. Not like a full panic, necessarily, but it sort of sits in my chest, like I can’t move on.

I’ll tell myself, “Just leave it, it’s fine,” and then I end up rereading the label text again, or nudging the same little objects on the table — the frame, the photo, whatever — and then checking the layout photos on my phone. Which is ridiculous because I know the layout photos don’t magically change. I actually have so many photos on my phone from projects, it’s kind of embarrassing… like half my storage is probably just near-identical shots of tables.

But with this piece, it’s not really documentation. It’s more like I keep checking until it feels settled. If I stop before that, I feel upset and distracted, and I just keep thinking about it instead of working. Part of me knows it’s already fine, but I still lose studio time going back to it.
How much time do these checking behaviors and thoughts take up in your day, and have they affected your ability to get things done or caused you significant distress?

It depends on the day, but… it’s not taking over my whole life, I guess. I’m still getting most of my work done. Like, I can still finish pieces, still show up to the studio.

But it does eat up more time than I want to admit. I’ll lose chunks of studio time to checking and rechecking, and then suddenly the afternoon is gone. And it has mattered. I missed a grant deadline because I kept getting stuck instead of just finishing the materials, and I backed out of a gallery talk I’d actually wanted to do, which still makes me feel kind of stupid.

I mean, I tell myself artists are always fussy about details — I had a professor who used to spend, like, three days deciding where to put one nail in a wall — but this doesn’t feel like that. It’s distressing. Not catastrophic every day, but enough that it’s interfering.

When you were working on this memorial piece, did these intrusive thoughts and checking behaviors happen only when you were focused on the artwork, or have you noticed them happening in other situations, even when you’re not working on the piece?

It was mostly around the memorial piece, yeah. That’s what made me come in, really. When I was working on it, I kept getting these awful thoughts that I was going to dishonor my aunt somehow — like if I chose the wrong photo, or put it in the wrong place, or picked a color that felt off, it meant I didn’t love her enough.

And I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud. I’ve made personal work before, and there’s always some second-guessing, like, “Is this too dark, is this too sentimental,” you know. I had this whole phase in school where I overthought every shade of blue for a series, which is not really the point, sorry.

But this felt different. I couldn’t just brush it off as normal creative doubt. It felt unwanted and really upsetting, like the thought would just stick there.
Have you noticed these intrusive thoughts or the urge to check things happening even when you’re not working on the memorial piece — like in other parts of your life or with other tasks?

Honestly, it’s mainly the memorial piece. That’s what brought me in. I mean, I can be fussy with other work too — like I once spent way too long deciding whether a tiny bit of shadow in a print looked “heavy,” and then of course no one else could even tell — but this felt different.

With my aunt’s piece, the thoughts were just… awful and unwanted. Like if I chose the wrong photo, or placed it wrong, or picked a color that didn’t feel right, it somehow meant I was dishonoring her, or that I didn’t love her enough. And I knew, logically, that a color choice doesn’t prove something like that. But I couldn’t just shrug it off the way I usually can with normal art doubts. It stuck.
Have you noticed any similar intrusive thoughts or urges to check or redo things in other parts of your life, even if they haven’t been as intense as with the memorial piece?

I mean… not really in the same way. I keep circling back to the memorial piece because that’s what scared me enough to come here. With that, it wasn’t just “oh, this composition isn’t working,” which happens all the time in art school and studios — like, you can spend an entire afternoon moving one object two inches and convince yourself it matters.

But this was more like… if I chose the wrong photo of my aunt, or put it in the wrong place, or used a color that felt wrong, then somehow I was dishonoring her. Like it meant I didn’t love her enough. And I knew that didn’t make sense, but I couldn’t just brush it off the way I usually can with normal creative doubts. It felt awful and unwanted, and it just stuck there.
Have you ever experienced similar intrusive thoughts or felt the need to check or redo things when you’re not working on the memorial piece — like in everyday situations or with other tasks?

I know you’re asking about outside the piece, and I’m trying to think of an example, but honestly the thing that keeps coming up is the memorial work.

That’s really why I came in. When I was working on my aunt’s piece, I’d get these horrible, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like if I chose the wrong photo, or placed it a little wrong, or picked a color that didn’t feel right, it would mean I didn’t love her enough.

And I can overthink artwork normally — I mean, I’ve spent ridiculous amounts of time on tiny details no one else notices — but this didn’t feel like that. I couldn’t just laugh it off or move on. It felt stuck in my head.
